video_caption: The video segment displays a presentation screen. Initially, the screen features the title "Formation of Bonds" in a blue box. Below this, it includes text with website addresses and credits for the script, narration, and animation, along with the date "27 June 2013." This introductory screen transitions to one showing the "Learning Objectives," stating the tutorial will cover adding bonds to existing bonds, orienting bonds, adding stereochemical bonds, and inverse wedge hashes. A subsequent screen lists the "System Requirement" as Ubuntu Linux OS version 12.04 and GChemPaint version 0.12.10. Finally, the last screen discusses "Pre-requisites", it indicates that viewers should be familiar with GChemPaint's chemical structure editor, and directs to the Spoken-Tutorial.org website for relevant tutorials if not. The background of these screens is a gradient of light green to white.

The video segment shows a computer screen displaying the 'EasyChem' application, featuring an ethane structure with H3C connected to CH3 in the drawing area. The right side of the screen showcases a toolbar with various tools and options for creating chemical structures, including buttons for drawing lines, arrows, shapes, and text. Below the toolbar, there are settings such as 'Current element: C' and adjustable properties like 'Bond length' and 'Bond angle'. A checkbox labeled 'Merge with existing atoms' is selected. There are no people visible in the video. The environment is a digital interface showing the software's features for chemical structure drawing.

The video segment shows a person demonstrating how to copy and paste an ethane structure using a software program. Initially, an ethane structure (H3C-CH3) is visible on the left side of the display area. The demonstrator uses the "select one or more objects" tool on the right side of the screen to highlight the ethane structure, then utilizes the keyboard shortcuts Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V to copy and paste it twice. After pasting, two structures overlap each other. The user then moves the second overlapping structure aside by placing the cursor on it and dragging it away using the mouse. The video highlights the single bond between carbon atoms within the structures. No people are physically seen in the video, only the interface of the software program being used.

The video displays a digital tutorial on how to convert a single bond to a double bond in a chemical structure using a drawing program. There are no people visible; instead, the focus is on the graphical interface of the software. The screen shows three molecules written out, each represented as H3C-CH3, which is ethane. The narrator, without being seen, instructs the viewer to select a tool labeled "Add a bond or change the multiplicity of an existing" tool from the right sidebar. The cursor then clicks on the single bond between the two carbons in the second ethane molecule, transforming it into a double bond, and the formula is updated to H2C==CH2, now ethene. The narrator explains that this conversion also reduces the number of hydrogen atoms from six to four, reflecting the updated molecular structure. The background is plain white, with the toolbar displayed on the right side of the screen.

The video segment displays a computer screen displaying an example of chemical structures using an editor with drawing tools and a properties panel on the right side.  There are three chemical structures on the left of the screen, which are arranged horizontally. The first structure has text of “H3C – CH3” above it, the second structure has text of “H2C == CH2” above it, and the third structure has “H3C – CH3” above it. The program interface includes basic drawing tools like lines and shapes, and a properties panel that shows the "Current element" as "C" (carbon) and bond length and bond angle values. The narrator clicks the existing bond on the right structure, which changes from a single bond to a triple bond, and text for structure is modified to “HC ≡ CH”. The narrator describes this process, explaining that a single bond gets converted to a triple bond, and the number of hydrogen atoms reduces from 6 to 2.

The video shows a screen recording of a chemistry drawing software. Initially, three chemical structures are displayed: Ethane (H3C-CH3), Ethene (H2C=CH2), and Ethyne (HC≡CH), each labeled with its name. The user presses "Ctrl+A" to select all objects, resulting in each structure being highlighted with a blue outline. Then, the user clicks on the "Select one or more objects" tool on the right-hand panel. Finally, the user drags all structures over to the right side of the screen. The background is a plain white canvas, indicating a virtual, software-based environment. The screen also contains the software's interface elements such as menu options, toolbars, and font selections.

The video segment is a chemistry educational resource. Initially, the screen displays the title "Structures" in large, blue letters at the top left. Below it is the title "Tetrahedral Methane Structure" in brown text, with a 2D chemical diagram of methane. An arrow shows the distance from the carbon atom to one of the hydrogen atoms labeled with "1.09 Å". The angle of one of the hydrogen bonds is measured at "109.5°". The presenter's name, "Madhuri Ganpathi", is written at the bottom with the text "Formation of Bonds". The scene transitions to a 3D molecular model of methane, shown against a grayish-green background. Each bond angle in this 3D model of methane is shown with the measurement of "109.5°". The segment concludes with a screen capture of the molecular model along with icons for drawing chemical diagrams. Next to it is "H3C--CH3 Ethane", "H2C=CH2 Ethene", and "HC=CH Ethyne".

The video presents a screen recording of a software program used for drawing chemical structures. The user is demonstrating how to create an Ethane structure. Initially, three chemical structures with labels, "Ethane," "Ethene," and "Ethyne," appear at the top of the screen. The user selects the "Add a bond or change the multiplicity of the existing one" tool from a toolbox on the right side and draws a horizontal bond in the central area of the screen. Subsequently, the user draws three bonds originating from each end of the horizontal bond, orienting them in different directions to simulate a tetrahedral geometry. To add hydrogen atoms at the ends of the bonds, the user presses the "H" key, selects "H" from the sub-menu that appears, selects the "Add or modify an atom" tool and adds "H" for hydrogen at each of the bond ends. The process results in a displayed structure that represents the Ethane molecule in the drawing area. No people are visible in the recording; the focus is strictly on the interaction with the software interface.

Here is a description of the video segment:

The screen recording displays a computer interface of a chemical drawing program called GChemPaint. At the top of the screen, the names of three chemical compounds are displayed: "H3C-CH3 Ethane" (Ethane), "H2C=CH2 Ethene" (Ethene), and "HC≡CH Ethyne" (Ethyne), all written in black. Below the chemical names are two structural diagrams. In the right-hand side of the screen is a menu with tools and settings of GChemPaint. The video describes the function of the "invert wedge hashes" option in the preferences menu, located in the "Edit" dropdown menu. Selecting this option adjusts the appearance of hashed bonds in the drawn structures, reversing the default convention where the narrower end of the hashed bond indicates the bond start. The recording highlights this function with an active cursor and emphasizes the difference in visual representation when the "invert wedge hashes" box is checked and unchecked.

The video segment depicts a computer screen displaying a chemistry drawing software interface. The screen shows two chemical structures with the labels "H3C--CH3 Ethane" ("H3C--CH3 Ethane") and "H2C==CH2 Ethene" ("H2C==CH2 Ethene") respectively. Below these are depictions of these molecules, as well as "H...H" ("H...H") at the bottom of the screen. A menu is on the right, containing various tools for drawing chemical structures, including different types of bonds and shapes. The current element is set to "H" (Hydrogen). A mouse cursor is used to click on the "add a hash bond" tool in the menu, then clicks on the bonds of the ethane molecule, specifically the carbon hydrogen bonds on the right side of the molecule, changing them into hash bonds.
